content:
A hospital appointment can take a whole day when arthritis makes walking, sitting and waiting painful, but most of the hard parts can be planned for. Ask the clinic before the day for the adjustments you need, such as a ground-floor room, an early slot, a wheelchair at the entrance or a phone or video appointment instead. Ask your GP or hospital team whether you qualify for free non-emergency patient transport, check the hospital's parking rules for disabled people, and take your appointment letter, a list of your medicines and your questions. If you cannot get there, tell the clinic before the date rather than missing it. Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself before a test unless the clinic tells you to.

This guide is for anyone with arthritis who finds hospital outpatient appointments exhausting, and for the family or friends who go with them. If the appointment is for a blood test, see getting to blood tests when travel is hard. If it is your first rheumatology visit, see what happens at a rheumatology appointment. If you are being admitted to a ward, see what to pack for a hospital stay.

Before the day: ask for what you need

Hospitals can often make small changes if you ask in advance. Ring the number on your appointment letter, or ask your GP surgery to add a note to your referral. Things worth asking for:

  • A time that suits your joints. If you are stiff first thing, a late-morning slot may be easier. If you tire through the day, ask for an early one.
  • A phone or video appointment if the clinic does not need to examine you this time. Many follow-up appointments can be done this way.
  • Help getting from the entrance to the clinic. Ask whether the hospital lends wheelchairs at the main entrance, has volunteers or porters who can help, or runs a buggy service on large sites.
  • Somewhere you can sit properly. Low waiting-room chairs can be hard to get out of with hip or knee arthritis. Ask if there is a higher chair with arms, and say if you cannot stand in a queue.
  • Combining appointments. If you have several clinics or tests at the same hospital, ask whether they can be booked on the same day.
  • Information in a form you can use, such as large print, or a call instead of a letter if your hands make opening post hard.

Write down your questions in the days before. Pain and tiredness make it easy to forget what you meant to ask.

Getting there

The NHS says you will usually be expected to make your own way to non-emergency appointments, but there is help for people who need it.

  • Non-emergency patient transport (PTS). This is free transport for people whose medical condition means they need support on the journey or who find it difficult to walk. Eligibility is assessed, so ask your GP, the clinic or your local patient transport service well before the day, and explain clearly what your arthritis stops you doing, such as walking from a bus stop or getting in and out of a car.
  • Help with travel costs. If you receive certain benefits or are on a low income, the Healthcare Travel Costs Scheme may refund the cost of getting to specialist NHS appointments or tests you have been referred for. Keep tickets and receipts, and ask at the hospital how to claim. The NHS Low Income Scheme can help if you are not on a qualifying benefit.
  • Community transport. Local schemes often run door-to-door minibuses or volunteer drivers for people who cannot use buses easily. See community transport.
  • Lifts from family or friends. Ask early, and ask them to drop you at the main entrance before parking.

Parking if you drive or are driven

  • In England, government guidance says NHS hospitals should offer free parking to people in greatest need, which includes disabled people and frequent outpatient attenders. Check the hospital's website or ask at reception how to claim it, as each hospital runs its own system.
  • If you have a Blue Badge, bring it. If walking from the car park is a big barrier for you, you may be able to apply for one; see our Blue Badge guide.
  • Look up where the clinic is in the hospital before you go and which car park or drop-off point is closest. Large hospitals can mean a long walk from the entrance.
  • Leave extra time so you are not rushing, which is when trips and falls are more likely.

What to take with you

  • Your appointment letter and any test results or diary you have been asked to bring
  • A list of all your medicines, including ones you buy yourself, or the boxes. The NHS App can show your medicines if you use it
  • Your written questions and something to take notes with, or ask the person with you to take notes
  • Glasses, hearing aids and any splints or walking aids you use
  • Your usual painkillers and any medicines due during the day, plus water and a snack, as clinics often run late
  • A cushion if hard chairs hurt, and a layer you can put on or take off
  • Your phone, charged, with the clinic's number saved

Do not stop or change any medicine before a test unless the clinic has told you to in writing.

Eye clinic days

Many people with arthritis are seen in eye clinics, for example for checks linked to certain medicines or because inflammatory arthritis can affect the eyes. Eye tests often use drops that widen your pupils, which can blur your vision for some hours afterwards. Check your letter, do not plan to drive yourself home, and bring someone with you or book transport. Sunglasses can help with the glare on the way home.

On the day

  • Tell reception if you cannot sit for long or need to stand and move, so you are not missed when called.
  • Get up and move gently every half hour or so while you wait, if you can, to stop your joints stiffening.
  • If you need the toilet often, ask where it is when you arrive.
  • In the appointment, say what matters most to you first. It is fine to ask the doctor or nurse to slow down, repeat something or write it down.
  • Before you leave, check what happens next: whether you need tests, who will contact you and how you will get the results.

If you cannot get there

Ring the clinic as soon as you know, before the date. Explain why, for example a flare, an infection or no transport. Ask whether the appointment can be done by phone or video, or moved. Missing appointments without telling anyone can mean being discharged back to your GP and having to be referred again.

If something goes wrong, such as transport not arriving or not being given the adjustments you asked for, the hospital's Patient Advice and Liaison Service (PALS) can help sort it out.

For family and carers

  • Offer to come in with them, take notes and help remember questions, but let them speak for themselves unless they ask you to.
  • Help plan the journey and the walk inside the hospital, including where to rest.
  • If you care for someone regularly, you may be entitled to a carer's assessment.

When not to wait for the appointment

  • Call 999 for chest pain, sudden severe breathlessness, signs of a stroke, or a serious fall or injury.
  • Contact NHS 111 or your GP urgently for a hot, swollen joint with a high temperature, feeling very unwell on medicines that lower your immunity, or new confusion.
  • If your arthritis is getting much worse while you wait, contact your rheumatology advice line or GP rather than waiting for the date.

Common questions

Can I have a phone appointment instead?

Often, yes, for follow-ups that do not need an examination or test. Ask the clinic. If you need to be seen in person, ask what help is available to get there.

Who decides if I can have patient transport?

It is assessed against national criteria based on your medical needs and mobility, not your age. Ask your GP, clinic or local patient transport service.

Can someone come with me?

Usually, yes. Having someone with you can help with the journey, waiting and remembering what was said.
